explanations.explanation: Pure joy it is, friend. James says, “Consider it pure joy, my brothers, when you encounter trials of many kinds…” He doesn't say a little joy or a sprinkle of joy. He says PURE. I'd have bet money he'd say "grit your teeth," so he got me too.

I get the pull, because trials hurt and sorrow shows up fast. When the oven eats my cookies, I know that feeling well. But James tells his brothers to consider trials pure joy, and he doesn't mention sorrow in this verse at all. He gives his reason in the very next verse.

That's a natural guess, but James never calls these trials a punishment. He says, “Consider it pure joy, my brothers…” That's all he says about how to look at them. Trials of many kinds, and his answer is joy.

Perseverance, friend. James says the testing of your faith develops it. So the trial isn't just something to survive. It's building something in you. And in the next verse he tells his brothers to let that work finish.

I can see why you'd pick it, since people do get proud after a hard stretch. But James doesn't say that here. He says the testing of your faith develops perseverance. Pride never shows up in the verse.

Trials can sure feel scary, so that's an honest guess. But James says the testing of your faith develops perseverance, not fear. He's telling his brothers what the trial builds in them. Fear isn't on his list.

Mature and complete, baker. James says to allow perseverance to finish its work “so that you may be mature and complete, not lacking anything.” That's a full batch, golden all the way through. He's not talking about a half-finished thing.

Nice-sounding guess, but James doesn't promise money or honor here. He says perseverance finishes its work so that you may be “mature and complete, not lacking anything.” That's about who his brothers become, not what they collect. Later in this very passage, he even says riches fade.

Strong sounds good, but feared isn't anywhere in this letter. James says perseverance finishes its work so that you may be “mature and complete, not lacking anything.” Nobody's being scary in this verse. It's all about being complete.
God is the one to ask. James says, “Now if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God…” Not a committee, not a group chat, just God. And he adds right away that God gives generously.
Elders can be a real help, but that's not what James says in this verse. He says, “Now if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God…” He points straight to God. No middleman needed.
A good teacher is a gift, I'll say that. But James doesn't send his brothers to a teacher here. He says anyone who lacks wisdom “should ask God.” And then he tells them how God gives.

True. James says God “gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him.” Generously, to ALL, with no fault-finding. So you can walk up and ask without rehearsing an apology first.

James actually says the opposite. He says God “gives generously to all without finding fault…” So God isn't stingy, and He isn't sitting there pointing out your mistakes before He answers. It's generous to all, and that's what the text says.

explanations.answer: A wave tossed by the wind
explanations.explanation: A wave, friend. James says the one who doubts “is like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind.” One minute up, one minute down, going wherever the wind pushes. That's a picture you can see in your head right away.

explanations.answer: A sheep lost from the flock
explanations.explanation: That's a picture people may know, but it isn't the one James uses here. For the person who doubts, he says, “…he who doubts is like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind.” The doubter gets pushed around, back and forth. A wave, not a sheep.

explanations.answer: A lamp hidden under a bowl
explanations.explanation: Good image, but it's not in this letter. James says the one who doubts “is like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind.” His picture is about being pushed around, not about hiding. So the answer is the wave.

James says the opposite. About the one who asks while doubting, he says, “That man should not expect to receive anything from the Lord.” So the doubter shouldn't expect to receive. That's what the text says.

False, and James is plain about it. He says, “That man should not expect to receive anything from the Lord.” The man he means is the one who asks while doubting. In the verse before, he's the wave that gets tossed around.

Low, baker. James says the humble brother should exult in his high position, “But the one who is rich should exult in his low position…” It's a switch. The humble one looks up, and the rich one gets pointed down.

Secure would sound comfy, but James doesn't say it. He says the rich one should exult in his low position. Comfy isn't the word anywhere in these verses. He actually follows it by saying the rich man will pass away.

Honored fits the humble brother better, since he's the one in a high position. For the rich one, James says to exult in his “low position.” He flips the two on purpose. So honored isn't the word he picks.

Right, because he will pass away. James says the rich man “will pass away like a flower of the field.” Then he describes the sun rising with scorching heat and withering the plant. His point is that the rich man will fade, in the midst of his pursuits.

explanations.answer: Because he must give it all away
explanations.explanation: That's an interesting thought, but James never says the rich man must give anything away. His reason is that “he will pass away like a flower of the field.” The flower falls and its beauty is lost. The verses stay on the fading.

explanations.answer: Because his riches are a test
explanations.explanation: James does talk about tests, but not here. His reason for the rich man is that “he will pass away like a flower of the field.” The sun comes up hot, the plant withers, and the flower falls. Nothing in these verses calls riches a test.

True. James says the man who perseveres under trial “will receive the crown of life that God has promised to those who love Him.” That's God's promise, not James's guess. And it comes after the man has stood the test.

James says the opposite. The man who perseveres under trial “will receive the crown of life that God has promised to those who love Him.” So the promise is real, and it's God's. The promise goes to those who love Him.

James says no to that. He writes, “When tempted, no one should say, ‘God is tempting me.’” Then he gives the reason: “For God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does He tempt anyone.” So it isn't fine to say it.

False, friend. James says, “When tempted, no one should say, ‘God is tempting me.’” His reason is that “God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does He tempt anyone.” Nobody gets to pass the blame upstairs.

His own evil desires. James says, “But each one is tempted when by his own evil desires he is lured away and enticed.” Each one means each one, so nobody gets a pass. That includes me and my love of chocolate chips.

People can sure push our buttons, but James doesn't name them here. He says each one is tempted “when by his own evil desires he is lured away and enticed.” It's about what's in the person himself. So the answer is his own desires.

Hard times are in this passage, since James opens with trials. But he doesn't say they're where temptation comes from. He says, “…each one is tempted when by his own evil desires he is lured away and enticed.” His own desires, not his circumstances.

It gives birth to death. James says, “Then after desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, gives birth to death.” He lays out the chain step by step: desire, sin, then death. It's a heavy verse, so no joke from me on this one.

explanations.answer: It fades away on its own
explanations.explanation: That would be nice, but James says something else. He says that sin, “when it is full-grown, gives birth to death.” It doesn't fade. It grows. It's a heavy verse, so I'll just say that plainly.

James doesn't say that. He says that sin, “when it is full-grown, gives birth to death.” Hidden isn't in the verse at all. He follows desire to sin and sin to death. It's a heavy one, and he states it plainly.

Above, baker. James says, “Every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights…” God tempts no one, and He gives every good and perfect gift. That's a good one to remember when you're feeling pulled around.

Within is where James puts temptation, not gifts. He says temptation comes from our own desires. Then he says, “Every good and perfect gift is from above…” So the gifts come down from the Father of the heavenly lights.

People do give us nice things, I won't argue with that. But James says, “Every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights…” He traces every good and perfect gift to the Father. So the answer is above.
The word of truth. James says, “He chose to give us birth through the word of truth…” The Father chose it and did it that way. And I love the word chose, since I know what it's like to be picked.
James doesn't point to our willpower. He says the Father “chose to give us birth through the word of truth.” The Father is the one doing the choosing. So the answer is the word of truth.

My mustache does plenty of work, but James doesn't credit our hands here. He says the Father “chose to give us birth through the word of truth…” It's the Father's choice, and the word of truth is how He did it. So hands are out.
